newsitem.title: CANADA: U.S. underscores trade gap worries with Japan.
newsitem.headline: U.S. underscores trade gap worries with Japan.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky voiced strong concerns about a potential rise in the U.S. trade deficit with Japan in a meeting on Thursday with Japan's trade and industry minister.

"We had a useful discussion focusing most particularly on the potential increase in the Japanese surplus with the United States," Barshefsky told reporters after an hour-long meeting with International Trade and Industry Minister Shinji Sato.

The two, in Toronto for a meeting of trade ministers of the four major industrial trading partners, discussed pressing issues including access to Japan's markets for automobiles, paper and agriculture and deregulation of Japan's economy.

U.S. officials said Barshefsky underscored Washington's concern about a potential widening of the trade gap after seeing it decline in recent years. She gave Sato a "strong message that it was important the hard-won progress of the last four years should not be reversed," one official said.

The U.S. trade deficit with Japan fell by 19 percent last year to nearly $48 billion, the lowest level since 1991. But U.S. manufacturers, particularly the Big Three car makers, have complained that the strong dollar, which makes U.S. goods expensive, and a weak yen, which makes Japanese goods cheaper in global markets, are hurting their business.

U.S. officials also expressed concern about a surge in automobile imports during the first few months of this year, and Barshefsky and U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin have warned Japan not to try to export its way out of recession.
"We've made progress over these four years, hard-won progress," a U.S. official told reporters. "It is important Japan keep moving forward and not slip back into old habits."

Discussions also centred on deregulation in Japan and Sato pledged to Barshefsky that Tokyo would carry out plans to cut bureaucratic red tape and lower costs to consumers. The United States is anxious the deregulation be done in a way that opens Japan's markets to more foreign competition.
They also discussed U.S. concerns about access to Japan's paper market. Japan's imports of paper dropped by 30 percent in recent months, a U.S. official said.
A market access agreement between the two countries expired last month but U.S. officials said it had been unsuccessful in opening Japan's market and they want to see more access for foreign firms.

The meeting between Barshefsky and Sato was one of a number of bilateral sessions during a two-day meeting of the so-call "Quad" -- the United States, Japan, European Union and Canada -- which offers the trade chiefs a chance to discuss a number of issues of concern including global negotiations on financial services markets and individual trade issues.

European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan chided Canada on Thursday about Canada's lack of action against the U.S. anti-Cuba legislation. "We put our head above the block and Canada has declined to do so," Brittan told reporters.

"I find it a little curious that we have gone ahead and challenged the Uhited States, taken a very high profile action and got some progress from the United States as a result of that, very substantial progress," he said. "And Canada has held back on (action through) NAFTA (the North American Free Trade Agreement)."

The European Union had challenged the United States in the World Trade Organisation over the U.S. Helms-Burton law, which set penalties against foreign firms for doing business in Cuba with property confiscated from U.S. citizens.

In April the European Commission and United States struck a deal under which the EC agreed to suspend action in the WTO and the White House to seek a change in the Helms-Burton law. The two parties agreed to discuss the confiscated property issue through the multilateral investment agreement under the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
"There'd been a sort of informal understanding of the division of labour, that we would go ahead under the WTO and Canada would go ahead under NAFTA," Brittan said.

But Canada has hesitated to challenge the Helms-Burton legislation under NAFTA. "I've still got the NAFTA challenge in my back pocket," Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton told reporters. "If things break down and don't proceed, then I can always use that."
